question: to the Commission Olivier Chastel (Renew) Subject:
Reports from a number of Member States and the European Court of Auditors have revealed that tens of billions of euros in e-commerce VAT and customs duties have gone uncollected. 1.

Does the Commission have an up-to-date estimate of the shortfall for the EU budget caused by major types of customs fraud for low-value and high-value business-toconsumer distance sales flows, as well as for business-to-business e-commerce flows where goods are sold after their arrival on EU soil?

Given the practical difficulties for national customs administrations to physically check millions of parcels every day, how does the Commission plan to modernise the reporting method applicable to business-to-consumer distance sales flows and to business-to-business e-commerce flows? What is the timetable for this?

To what extent does the Commission plan to integrate source-based data certification technologies to ensure that the amounts collected by online sales platforms actually correspond to the financial transactions carried out and to ensure the accuracy of customs declarations for all types of flows – including business-to-business e-commerce flows?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) The Commission annually publishes the value-added tax (VAT) Gap study, which estimated the EU VAT compliance gap for 2023 at EUR 128 billion. The methodology does not identify specific fraud types. Work with Member States is ongoing to develop methods to estimate VAT losses linked to e-commerce fraud. For customs duties, the Commission has no estimate of the shortfall in the EU budget. Further to the introduction of the EUR 3 temporary customs duty, the Commission shall assess by 1 October 2026 whether a diversion of trade flows occurs If needed the Commission can extend the scope of this duty to all goods with a value not exceeding EUR 150. Under the upcoming EU Customs Reform, operators will submit data to a new EU Customs Data Hub instead of separate national systems. Its first phase, covering e-commerce business-toconsumer supplies, is expected to start on 1 July 2028. This should improve data management and customs controls. The full Hub should be used by Trust and Check traders1 from March 2031 and by all operators from February 2034. From 1 July 2026, items in parcels worth up to EUR 150 sent from a third country to an EU consumer are subject to a temporary EUR 3 customs duty. In parallel, the Commission, together with e-commerce stakeholders and Member State experts, is developing a fast-track solution to strengthen the security of the Import One Stop Shop. From 1 November 2026, all distance sales will also be subject to an EU handling fee. The Commission also supports Eurofisc in using data from payment service providers to detect inconsistencies between payment flows and VAT declarations.
1 Customs authorities can grant this status to economic operators considered as highly trustworthy, because they

fulfil stricter criteria of legal, digital and operational compliance. These traders may enjoy specific benefits, e.g. no customs intervention to release or control the goods (‘green lane’), supervision by their Member States of establishment and no obligation to put the goods in transit.
